lead: A latent variable model says the data you see is produced by hidden causes you do not see. A photo of a face has pose, light and expression as hidden variables; pixels are observed. The model writes the joint density of hidden and observed variables, then sums or integrates the hidden part away to get p(x). Maximum likelihood chooses parameters that make the observed data most probable under that marginal. This idea underlies variational autoencoders, restricted Boltzmann machines and many generative models used for image editing and inpainting.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 probability and loss functions, and Chapter 6.1 for encoder-decoder notation.

sections.h3: Hidden cause, observed data, marginal likelihood

blocks.text: A latent variable model separates what is observed from what is hidden. Let x be the observed data: a pixel image, a word, or a cricket score. Let z be the latent variable: a compact hidden cause such as pose, topic or style. The parameter vector θ contains the model weights. The model gives a prior p(z) and a conditional p(x|z), often called the decoder. Their product is the joint density p(x,z)=p(z)p(x|z). The data density is the marginal p(x)=∫ p(z)p(x|z) dz, or p(x)=Σ_z p(z)p(x|z) when z is discrete. The sum or integral removes z, so only x remains.

For N independent observations x₁,...,x_N, maximum likelihood chooses θ to maximize log L(θ)=Σ_{i=1}^N log p(x_i;θ). This is the same as minimizing negative log-likelihood. The integral is often over many z dimensions and has no closed form. A Monte Carlo estimate draws M samples z_m~p(z) and uses p(x)≈(1/M)Σ_{m=1}^M p(x|z_m;θ). EM is an alternative: it iterates between a posterior over z and a parameter update. The estimate is noisy but unbiased for fixed θ.

A Markov network encodes independence through missing edges. A node is independent of all non-neighbouring nodes given its neighbours. In a latent-variable graph, z has no parent and x is its child. Conditional on z, x is independent of other latent causes not connected to it. This local independence assumption makes p(x|z) factorize.

A restricted Boltzmann machine is a latent-variable model with visible units v and hidden units h. Its energy is E(v,h)=-aᵀv-bᵀh-vᵀWh. Here a is the visible bias vector, b is the hidden bias vector, W is the weight matrix, and the superscript ᵀ means transpose. The joint probability is p(v,h)=exp(-E(v,h))/Z, where Z=Σ_{v,h} exp(-E(v,h)) is the partition function. To get p(v), sum over h: p(v)=Σ_h p(v,h). Because v and h form a bipartite graph with no visible-visible or hidden-hidden edges, conditional samples are easy: p(h|v) and p(v|h) factorize over units. Training usually uses contrastive divergence, which starts from data, samples h, reconstructs v, and moves parameters to lower the data energy relative to the reconstruction. Only a few universities require the full derivation.

sections.h3: What maximum likelihood does and does not mean

blocks.text: Maximum likelihood does not ask which single z produced a point. It asks how much probability the model assigns to x after summing over all z. Two models can have the same encoder p(x|z) and different priors p(z); their marginals differ. The likelihood also penalizes a model that puts high mass on hidden states that rarely produce the observed x.

Once trained, the model supports sampling and inference. To generate, draw z~p(z), then x~p(x|z). To edit, condition on part of x and infer plausible z. To evaluate, report average log-likelihood per data point, (1/N)Σ log p(x_i), or bits per pixel/dimension. On held-out data, a higher average log-likelihood means a better density model, though image quality can still be poor. Chapter 6.3 replaces the intractable integral with a learned lower bound. GANs in Chapter 6.4 avoid likelihood entirely.

examples.question: A latent variable z takes value 1 with probability 0.6 and value 2 with probability 0.4. Given z, a binary observation x has p(x=1|z=1)=0.9 and p(x=1|z=2)=0.2. Assume p(x=0|z)=1-p(x=1|z). (a) Find p(x=1) and p(x=0). (b) For observations [1,1,0], find the likelihood L and log-likelihood ln L. Use natural log.
steps: Prior: p(z=1)=0.6 and p(z=2)=0.4. These are dimensionless probabilities.
Log-likelihood: ln L=ln(0.146072)=-1.9237, which rounds to -1.924.
examples.check:
import math
p_z1 = 0.6
p_z2 = 0.4
p_x1_z1 = 0.9
p_x1_z2 = 0.2
p_x1 = p_z1 * p_x1_z1 + p_z2 * p_x1_z2
p_x0 = 1 - p_x1
L = p_x1 * p_x1 * p_x0
logL = math.log(L)
print(round(p_x1, 3))
print(round(p_x0, 3))
print(round(L, 3))
print(round(logL, 3))

traps: Do not maximize the joint p(x,z) for a guessed z and call it maximum likelihood of x. The likelihood of x needs the sum or integral over all z.
Do not use the prior p(z) as if it were the posterior p(z|x). The marginal p(x) weights p(x|z) by the prior p(z).
In a Monte Carlo estimate of p(x), sample z from the prior p(z), not from the posterior p(z|x), unless you correct with importance weights.
For binary x, remember p(x=0)=1-p(x=1). A common slip is to use p(x=1) again for the zero observation.
In an RBM, the joint has exp(-E), not exp(E), and Z sums over both visible and hidden states. A sign error reverses the probability ordering.

quiz.q: Define latent variable and observed variable in a latent-variable model.
quiz.a: Latent variable z is a hidden cause that is not observed. Observed variable x is the data. The model gives p(z) and p(x|z), and p(x)=Σ_z p(z)p(x|z) or the integral form.

quiz.q: Why can p(x)=∫p(z)p(x|z)dz be hard to compute?
quiz.a: The integral is over many latent dimensions, often has no closed form, and requires summing or integrating over many z values. Monte Carlo or variational methods approximate it.

quiz.q: A student fits by maximizing p(x,z) at z=1 for each point. Why is this not maximum likelihood of x?
quiz.a: It ignores other z values. The likelihood of x is the marginal sum over z, so maximizing one joint term can select parameters that do not maximize p(x).

quiz.q: M=3 Monte Carlo samples z=1,2,1 are drawn. The emissions are p(x=1|z=1)=0.9 and p(x=1|z=2)=0.2. Estimate p(x=1).
Write the RBM energy and joint probability, and define each symbol.
quiz.a: E(v,h)=-aᵀv-bᵀh-vᵀWh. Here v is visible units, h is hidden units, a is visible bias, b is hidden bias, W is weights, and ᵀ is transpose. p(v,h)=exp(-E(v,h))/Z, where Z=Σ_{v,h}exp(-E(v,h)).

quiz.q: In a Markov network, why is a node independent of non-neighbours given its neighbours?
quiz.a: By the local Markov property, every path to a non-neighbour passes through a neighbour. Conditioning on the neighbours blocks those paths, so the node is independent of non-neighbours.

beyond: Not for exam. Modern generative models replace the exact marginal with learned inference networks, Markov chain Monte Carlo, score matching or diffusion objectives. In industry, latent-variable thinking appears in recommendation embeddings, anomaly detection and image compression. Research directions include amortized variational inference, normalizing flows and diffusion models. Search terms: variational inference, expectation-maximization, contrastive divergence, evidence lower bound.
